title: Modes and typing
summary: Switch between Normal and Insert mode, type before or after the cursor, and open a new line.
body: Vim starts in Normal mode. There, keys are commands, not text: `x` deletes a character and `j` moves down. The line under the editor shows the mode, e.g. `-- NORMAL --`.
To type text, switch to Insert mode. `i` inserts before the cursor and `a` appends after it. `I` and `A` do the same at the start and at the end of the line.
`o` opens a new line below the cursor and `O` one above it, both ready for typing.
`<Esc>` always brings you back to Normal mode. Most tasks expect you to finish there.

keys.does: Insert at the first non-blank character of the line
Append at the end of the line

title: Moving the cursor
summary: Move by characters and lines, and jump to the ends of a line and of the file.
body: In Normal mode, `h`, `j`, `k` and `l` move the cursor left, down, up and right. They sit under your right hand, so you need not reach for the arrow keys.
A number before a motion repeats it: `3l` moves three characters to the right and `2j` two lines down.
`0` goes to the first column of the line, `^` to its first non-blank character and `$` to its last character.
`gg` jumps to the first line of the file and `G` to the last one. With a number, `G` goes to that line: `5G` is line 5.

keys.does: First non-blank character of the line

title: Editing single characters
summary: Replace, delete and change the case of one character, and change a number.
body: Many fixes touch a single character, and Vim has a command for each of them that keeps you in Normal mode.
`r` followed by a character replaces the character under the cursor: `ra` puts an `a` there. `x` deletes the character under the cursor and `X` the one before it.
`~` switches the case of the character under the cursor and moves on, so `~~~` switches three.
`<C-a>` adds one to the number under or after the cursor and `<C-x>` subtracts one. A count changes it by more: `5<C-a>` adds five.

keys.does: Replace the character under the cursor with a
Delete the character under the cursor
Delete the character before the cursor
Switch the case of the character and move on

title: Words
summary: Move by words: to the start of the next word, to the end of a word, and back.
body: Moving one character at a time is slow. Word motions jump over whole words.
`w` goes to the start of the next word, `e` to the end of the current or the next word, and `b` back to the start of the previous one.
Punctuation is a word of its own: after `end` in `end.`, `w` stops at the `.`. `W`, `E` and `B` treat everything between spaces as one word.
Counts work here too: `2w` skips two words. Letters with accents, like the `é` in `café`, belong to the word.

keys.does: The same, with words separated by spaces only

title: Lines
summary: Open, delete, copy and move whole lines.
body: Doubling an operator makes it work on the whole line: `dd` deletes the current line and `yy` copies (yanks) it.
`p` puts what you deleted or copied after the cursor; for whole lines, that is below the current line. `P` puts it above.
So `ddp` swaps a line with the one below it, and `yyp` duplicates a line.
`o` and `O` open a new line below or above, ready for typing.

keys.does: Put below the line (after the cursor for characters)
Swap the line with the next one

title: Search
summary: Find a character in the line, search the file for a pattern, and go to the next match.
body: `f` followed by a character moves to its next occurrence in the line: `fx` jumps to the next `x`. `t` stops just before it, and `F` and `T` look backwards.
`;` repeats the last `f` or `t`, and `,` repeats it in the other direction.
`/` searches the whole file: type a pattern and press `<CR>`. `?` searches backwards. `n` goes to the next match and `N` to the previous one.
Search is case-sensitive here, and patterns use Vim's syntax: `/\<cat\>` finds the word `cat` but not `cats`.

keys.does: Repeat the last f or t

title: Operators and counts
summary: Combine an operator with a motion, and use counts to reach further.
body: Commands such as `d` (delete), `c` (change) and `y` (yank) are operators: they wait for a motion and act on the text it moves over.
`dw` deletes to the start of the next word, `d$` to the end of the line, and `dj` deletes the current line and the next one.
`c` works the same way but leaves you in Insert mode to type the replacement. Some pairs have a shortcut: `D` is `d$` and `C` is `c$`.
A count can go before the operator or the motion: `2dd` and `d2d` both delete two lines, and `d3w` deletes three words.

keys.does: Delete to the end of the line
Change to the end of the line
Delete this line and the next

title: Registers
summary: Copy into named registers, keep a copy while deleting, and put whole lines.
body: Every delete and yank goes into a register. Without a name, it is the unnamed register `"`, which `p` puts back.
Type `"` and a letter before a command to use a named register: `"ayiw` copies a word into register `a`, and `"ap` puts it.
A register remembers whether it holds characters or whole lines; lines are always put on lines of their own, wherever the cursor is in the line.
Deleting overwrites the unnamed register. To delete without losing what you copied, delete into the black hole register: `"_dd`.

keys.does: Copy the word into register a
Copy two lines into register b
Copy a line and put it below the next one
Delete the line without touching any register

title: Text objects
summary: Act on a whole word, or on the inside of quotes, brackets and tags, from wherever the cursor is in them.
body: After an operator, `i` and `a` select a text object around the cursor. `iw` is the word under the cursor, whatever its position in the word; `aw` also takes the space after it.
`ciw` changes the whole word, so the cursor does not have to be at its start. `diw` deletes it.

The same works for pairs: `i"` is the inside of the quotes, `i(` the inside of the parentheses and `it` the inside of an HTML tag. `a"`, `a(` and `at` also take the quotes, the parentheses or the tags.
`ci"cat<Esc>` replaces the quoted text and keeps the quotes. `di(` empties the innermost pair of parentheses around the cursor.

keys.does: Change the word under the cursor
Delete the word, or the word and its space
Delete the quotes and what is inside

title: Visual selection
summary: Select characters or lines, see the area, and run an operator on it.
body: `v` starts selecting characters at the cursor and `V` whole lines. Motions then extend the selection, and it is highlighted, so you see exactly what an operator will touch.
Both ends are included: `vwe`, started on the `b` of `beta` in `alpha beta gamma`, selects up to the last `a` of `gamma`.
With a selection, an operator acts on it at once: `d` deletes it, `y` copies it, `>` indents the lines and `~` switches the case.
`o` jumps to the other end of the selection and `<Esc>` ends it. Some tasks want the selection still active at the end: press Check, or Alt+Enter, while it is.

keys.does: Go to the other end of the selection
Delete, copy, indent, switch case of the selection

title: Undo and redo
summary: Take a change back with undo and bring it back with redo.
body: `u` undoes the last change and `<C-r>` redoes it. A change is one Normal-mode command together with everything typed in the Insert mode it started: `ifoo<Esc>` is undone by a single `u`.
Undo walks back through your changes one by one, and redo forward again, until you make a new change.
`:undo` and `:redo` do the same from the command line.
In these tasks the judge checks the way, not only the result: typing a deleted `!` again gives the same text, but it is not an undo.

keys.does: Undo and redo from the command line

title: Formatting
summary: Join lines, indent them, and change the case of words and lines.
body: `J` joins the next line to the current one with a single space between them; `gJ` joins without adding a space. With a count, `3J` joins three lines.
`>>` indents the line by one level and `<<` takes the indent back; here one level is two spaces. With a selection, `>` and `<` indent every selected line.
`gU`, `gu` and `g~` are operators that make text uppercase, lowercase or switch its case: `gUiw` uppercases a word. Doubled, they act on the line: `g~~` switches the case of the whole line.

keys.does: Join with the next line, with one space
Indent the line, or take the indent back
Switch the case of the line
